stories.title: Vermont Has Spent Nearly a Billion Dollars to Clean Up Lake Champlain. But the Green Slime Keeps Coming Back.
stories.summary: The post Vermont Has Spent Nearly a Billion Dollars to Clean Up Lake Champlain. But the Green Slime Keeps Coming Back. appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.imageAlt: Green water floats near the edge of a rocky shore under a blue sky. A dock with an Adirondack chair, a house and trees can be seen in the distance.
stories.body:
Co-published with Seven Days

Reporting Highlights

Falling Behind: After a decade and nearly a billion dollars, the EPA says Vermont is “not on track” to meet its phosphorus reduction goals.

Some Parts Getting Worse: Seven of Lake Champlain’s 15 sampling stations have exceeded the EPA’s annual phosphorus limits every year since 2015.

Policies Pushed Back: Vermont has delayed tightening farm regulations, requiring property owners to control stormwater and fixing a system in which two agencies oversee farm pollution.

These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

On the last day of August, Jeff van den Noort spotted thick swirls of neon green film coating the water just steps from his home in Vermont. He waded in up to his ankles and dipped a jar to get a sample of the scum.

It wasn’t the first time he’d seen the slime. Since his parents bought the house on an island in Lake Champlain in 1966, van den Noort has spent part of nearly every summer in this quiet spot. Back then, the lake was clear.

But he began to witness the water’s deterioration as he grew older, especially after he moved into the home full time in 2010 to care for his ailing mother. That day in late August was the worst he’d seen all summer.

Later that week, van den Noort grabbed a bucket, a few Mason jars and a smartphone and got into his rusty Saab. He drove past the boat launches, frozen-in-time general stores and windswept pastures of the lake’s islands in northern Vermont and stopped at four other spots along the shore. Each time, he collected some murky water, gauged how thick the muck was, took a few photos and jotted down the weather conditions. He then uploaded his report to an online database.

Van den Noort was one part of a large volunteer effort to monitor a problem that has plagued Lake Champlain, which supplies drinking water to about 200,000 people. In recent decades, blooms of potentially toxic cyanobacteria, often called blue-green algae, have killed pets, forced beaches to close and hurt business and property values along the shores of this iconic Vermont feature.

“I just don’t feel like enough is being done,” van den Noort said. “And I think the state needs to take this seriously.”

Just over a decade ago, state leaders seemed to be doing just that. In 2015, then-Gov. Peter Shumlin stood a few feet from Lake Champlain by the Burlington waterfront and signed Vermont’s Clean Water Act. It promised to tighten limits on pollution and provide funding to clean up the state’s waterways.

The move was a response to ratcheting pressure from environmentalists and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. The EPA had been telling Vermont officials for years that they needed to take much stronger action. In 2016, the agency finalized tougher cleanup targets that the state must meet by 2036.

But after 10 years and nearly a billion dollars spent on water quality projects and programs, Vermont’s cleanup effort is faltering. In a little-noticed letter to the head of Vermont’s Department of Environmental Conservation last year, the EPA’s regional administrator warned that the state was “not on track” to meet its cleanup goal and would need to more than double its annual pace.

Halfway through the two-decade timetable, Vermont has achieved only 35% of the goal, according to the state’s most recent estimates. And the steps that Vermont has taken to get there, such as upgrading sewage treatment plants, represent “low-hanging fruit,” Eric Perkins, a former EPA official involved in setting the target, wrote in an email in response to questions from Seven Days and ProPublica.

The culprit behind these blooms is phosphorus, an element that is an essential building block of life, present in all organic matter. But too much of it has been pouring into the lake from farm fields saturated with fertilizer and manure, dirty stormwater, and raw sewage from treatment plants overwhelmed by heavy rains. That has tipped the lake’s ecosystem out of balance, spurring the growth of microorganisms that turn shallow bays and shorelines into no-go zones.

Ingesting cyanobacteria-laden water can cause vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness and liver damage, while skin contact can lead to rashes. Researchers have also detected possible links between chronic exposure to cyanobacteria and heightened risk of Parkinson’s disease and ALS, also known as Lou Gehrig’s disease. The algae blooms can also deprive fish and other aquatic life of oxygen.

While some areas of Lake Champlain have seen incremental improvements in phosphorus concentrations and cyanobacteria blooms, other parts of the lake are getting worse. Seven of the lake’s 15 sampling stations have exceeded the EPA’s annual phosphorus limits every year since 2015, a Seven Days and ProPublica analysis of lake monitoring data through 2025 shows. Four stations recorded higher average phosphorus levels over the past decade than in the decade before, including in the southern part of the lake and its northeast arm.

In September, the Department of Environmental Conservation reported to the EPA that in two northeastern sections of the lake most chronically plagued by phosphorus runoff, the state is not nearly on track to meet its targets. The department specifically acknowledged that it was not making enough progress in addressing stormwater runoff and that reductions in farm pollution in the Missisquoi River watershed have slowed since 2023.

Vermont shares the 120-mile-long lake with New York and Quebec, but it’s the source of about two-thirds of the phosphorus that flows into the water body. Agriculture is the largest polluting sector, while stormwater runoff from development, like urban parking lots and rural roads, contributes the highest amount of phosphorus per acre.

State agencies have repeatedly delayed taking more difficult and politically fraught action to crack down on pollution from farms, businesses and housing developments. Policies around them have encountered resistance from the dairy industry, property owners and lawmakers sympathetic to their interests.

The challenges in cleaning up Lake Champlain raise a salient question: If a small, conservation-minded state like Vermont can’t tackle this problem, what does that mean for other areas of the United States grappling with algae blooms in the Great Lakes, the Chesapeake Bay and the Gulf of Mexico?

State officials counsel patience as they remind Vermonters it will take more time to solve the problem.

“We are moving apace with the commitments we’ve made, in terms of the projects, but it isn’t manifesting itself nearly as quickly in the lake monitoring data,” said Julie Moore, Agency of Natural Resources secretary. “This is a complex ecosystem, and we need to come at this work with a whole lot of humility.”

Leaders of the Agency of Agriculture, Food and Markets said it will take time for investments, such as programs to reduce soil erosion and help farmers upgrade their manure storage equipment, to pay off.

“The first five years, we were really developing an enormous amount of programs,” said Laura DiPietro, the agency’s water quality program director, but implementing them “doesn’t happen overnight.” She said she expects to see greater phosphorus reductions resulting from them in the coming decade.

But for van den Noort, the blooms are increasingly hard to ignore.

“The worst days ever are really, really bad,” he said. “Just as far as you can see, the whole bay is green.”

Pushing the Limits

Unlike chemicals and heavy metals, which can be removed from lakes and rivers with dredging, phosphorus isn’t technically or economically feasible to extract.

So environmental regulators focus instead on limiting the amount of phosphorus that flows into the water each day. It’s like putting the lake on a diet. The EPA sets what’s known as the total maximum daily load, a target based on the agency’s determination of how much phosphorus the lake can absorb and remain healthy. To meet that goal, the state must cut pollution from agriculture, stormwater drains, roads, forests and wastewater treatment plants.

The EPA had set previous targets for Lake Champlain in 2002, but, concerned that Vermont wasn’t taking strong enough measures, the agency set tougher ones in 2016. For the first few years after those targets were updated, Perkins, who was then the EPA’s Vermont water quality coordinator, felt that the state was generally on the right track.

During his tenure, state agencies and lawmakers set up the Clean Water Fund to finance water quality projects and dedicated tax revenue streams to support it. They put in place stronger rules for fertilizer use and manure storage on farms. They created permit programs to limit stormwater runoff from roads and municipalities. That progress was reflected in a 2020 report card the EPA issued, acknowledging that Vermont had checked off all the milestones up to that point.

“Overall, I was very impressed with the level of commitment demonstrated by the state,” Perkins wrote to Seven Days and ProPublica.

By the time Perkins retired in 2021, he and colleagues at the EPA had become concerned about signs of lagging commitment by Vermont’s agencies to water quality enforcement on farms.

One clear opportunity to speed up phosphorus reductions, according to Perkins, is to ensure farms comply with required agricultural practices and avoid spreading manure before anticipated rainstorms, which has caused “major phosphorus runoff events.”

If the state and farm operators were to make that a priority, “it could likely make a big difference,” Perkins wrote. And the state could encourage that practice by overhauling its permitting system to tighten water quality requirements and enforcement for farms that keep animals confined in barns for long periods of time. Those farms are called concentrated animal feeding operations, or CAFOs. In recent years, many small family dairies in Vermont have closed or consolidated into larger operations that would be considered CAFOs under federal law.

Yet Vermont has delayed action on an EPA directive to strengthen its approach to regulating CAFOs. Just across the lake, New York has used such permits for decades to ensure better environmental practices on larger farms. In Vermont, a recent state task force report recommended working to develop this program for another five years.

A second, related reform the EPA has recommended is to change who leads regulation of those farms.

Vermont has two different agencies that oversee farm pollution. The Agency of Agriculture regulates how farms handle waste on site, while the Agency of Natural Resources is responsible if runoff from that waste leaves the farm. This split responsibility has caused oversight problems, including lapses in following up on reported water quality violations with inspections and enforcement actions. Environmental advocates have long maintained that the agriculture agency has a conflict because it also has a mandate to promote the state’s farm sector.

This arrangement frustrates farmers, too. In a letter to Gov. Phil Scott earlier this year, owners of one Vermont dairy farm wrote that “the lack of alignment and clear communication between these agencies” places farmers in an uncertain position. “Many in the farming community feel caught in the middle of interagency disagreements, unsure which standards will ultimately govern their operations or how enforcement will proceed,” they wrote.

In interviews, officials at the two agencies acknowledged those communication problems but said that they have taken steps to improve how they share information on potential violations and coordinate more closely on inspections.

In 2024, the EPA ordered Vermont to consolidate the regulation of agricultural pollution under the Agency of Natural Resources, Vermont’s main environmental agency, which the EPA says has sole authority to administer federal Clean Water Act rules.

In a letter that year to Moore, the agency’s secretary, EPA Region 1 administrator David Cash noted that the EPA had monitored the situation in Vermont for well over a decade. “And despite having had ample time and opportunity to cure longstanding program deficiencies,” he wrote, “ANR has failed to do so.” Cash noted that the state has failed to give ANR “sufficient resources or operational authority” to regulate runoff from farms.

Hovering over this back-and-forth is the threat that the federal government could take over enforcement of water pollution rules from Vermont.

Do You Live Near Lake Champlain? Help Seven Days and ProPublica Investigate Algae Blooms.

Seven Days and ProPublica have teamed up to investigate the cleanup of Lake Champlain. Have you been affected by this issue? We’d like to hear from you.

Following the letter to Moore, the divisions between the two agencies were on display as they discussed their regulatory approach in internal emails obtained under Vermont’s Public Records Act by Seven Days and ProPublica. In a 2025 email, Agency of Natural Resources general counsel Catherine Gjessing reminded her counterpart at the agriculture agency and legislative counsel staff that “there are a significant number of farms that are in fact discharging without a permit” in violation of the federal Clean Water Act. She added that the two agencies had been working under this split responsibility arrangement, with the agriculture agency taking the lead, “for decades now and we are still not in compliance.”

In an interview, the agriculture agency’s general counsel, Steve Collier, said there was never “a Wild West situation where farms were not being regulated” and that his agency’s rules protected the environment. “Whether or not the Clean Water Act was being administered exactly as it should be is a different issue,” he said.

Outside of agriculture, Vermont has yet to fully implement a third EPA demand as well as the directives of its own Clean Water Act. That 2015 law mandated the Department of Environmental Conservation to require properties with 3 or more acres of paved surface, such as parking lots, to install systems to slow and capture stormwater runoff.

Five years later, when the department still hadn’t finalized this “3-acre rule” permit system, the EPA warned Vermont that it would have to give the state “a failing grade” if it didn’t do so by Sept. 4, 2020. Vermont met the EPA’s deadline but in 2025 passed a law pushing the date for getting permits to 2028 for properties in the Champlain basin.

And those property owners don’t need to make the stormwater upgrades until 2033.

Treading Water

For a quarter century, Steve Cushing has been advocating to clean up St. Albans Bay in the northeast part of Lake Champlain near the epicenter of Vermont’s dairy industry. Throughout that time, he listened as federal and state environmental officials came through town and pledged to act. “Expect a lot of progress 10 years from now in many segments of the lake,” one EPA official told him and his neighbors in 2015 .

A decade later, this summer’s cyanobacteria blooms in the shallow bay were some of the worst he’s seen in several years, he said. Since June, the public beach in the St. Albans Bay Park has mostly been closed to swimming.

“Overall, you can’t really see a big improvement in water quality in the bay,” Cushing said.

Public data supports that notion. Every three years the federally funded Lake Champlain Basin Program, which coordinates research and grantmaking across the lake’s watershed, issues a report summarizing its water quality monitoring.

Its most recent edition, from 2024, revealed “deteriorating” trends in the northeast arm of the lake for both phosphorus and cyanobacteria and no progress in Missisquoi Bay, a shallow stretch spanning the U.S.-Canada border that frequently suffers intense blooms.

That’s troubling, scientists and advocates say, because the failure to address new pollution is exacerbated by both historical pollution and the effects of climate change.

What scientists call “legacy phosphorus” has accumulated in soils and lake sediments after many decades of fertilizer use, manure spreading, deforestation and unregulated septic and wastewater systems.

“We are working on a system that’s been impacted by human activities for the past 150-plus years,” said Matthew Vaughan, the chief scientist of the basin program.

Climate change poses another headwind for the lake cleanup. Since 2003, cyanobacteria blooms have appeared earlier in the spring and later in the fall as temperatures rise, and even at lower phosphorus levels. The drought that hit Vermont in 2025 led to a spike in blooms, thanks to the combination of heat and low water levels. Meanwhile, downpours are turning Vermont’s streams and rivers into fire hoses of phosphorus-laden sediment: In just one week in July 2023, record-shattering floods pumped six months worth of phosphorus into the lake.

“All of this just makes it more urgent to do our part to address these water quality challenges,” Vaughan said.

Some state officials and researchers contend that phosphorus deposited in the lake bed and soil decades ago might play as significant a role in fueling algae blooms as today’s runoff.

But while legacy phosphorus remains a challenge, “I think it’d be wrong to just rely on that as the excuse,” said Eric Smeltzer, who worked for the Department of Environmental Conservation for 35 years, including as the state limnologist who monitors the health of Vermont’s lakes and ponds.

“The most important technical question about the Lake Champlain phosphorus cleanup is: Are these practices working? And if not, why not?” Smeltzer said. “How can it be done better? I think you can’t just explain it away based on time lags and legacy phosphorus forever.”

In reviewing the state’s data recently, one detail in particular jumped out to him, he said. Wastewater treatment still garners an outsize share of Vermont’s clean water spending, even though it has been clear for years that it’s not a major contributor of phosphorus, while agriculture and stormwater are.

Read More

Cushing traces the algae blooms back to the dairy farms that dominate the watershed and to regulators’ failure to “put any teeth behind” restrictions on manure spreading and other water quality rules.

Cushing, a former dairy farmer, has pushed for policy changes as a volunteer with the St. Albans Area Watershed Association and has led an effort to mechanically remove vegetation that contributes to the phosphorus problem in his overburdened bay.

At 78, he is now searching for someone to take over the weed removal effort. “I’m getting a little burned out,” he admitted.

Seven miles to the west, on the island of North Hero, van den Noort questioned this summer whether all the data he gathers is making any difference.

“If we really wanted to solve the problem, I think we’d have to make some tough choices,” he said. “I don’t think anybody wants to do that. It’s a head-in-the-sand thing.”

Every week, van den Noort drives up the western edge of Isle La Motte on his monitoring circuit, looking out over a stretch of water that is supposed to be one of the cleanest parts of Lake Champlain. On the worst days, a pea green broth of blooms stubbornly hugs its entire shoreline.

stories.title: Vermont Was Supposed to Get an Audit of Its Lake Champlain Cleanup. It Never Happened.
stories.summary: The post Vermont Was Supposed to Get an Audit of Its Lake Champlain Cleanup. It Never Happened. appeared first on ProPublica .

stories.imageAlt: Two children wearing swim trunks wade into water. A small white sailboat appears near the horizon.
stories.body:
Halfway through a 20-year push to get Vermont’s waterways in line with tougher EPA standards, some lawmakers worry the project’s strategies aren’t as cost-effective as they could be — especially as a state-mandated audit was never done.

Co-published with Seven Days

This summer, Vermont’s Clean Water Board celebrated a milestone: Over the past decade, the state has invested nearly a billion dollars to clean up its polluted streams, rivers and lakes. The vast majority of that money has gone toward Lake Champlain.

“I think that’s something to be extremely proud of,” said Douglas Farnham, the board’s chair.

Vermont was supposed to get an independent evaluation of what it has gotten for all that money. But that study was never done.

A decade ago, Vermont lawmakers mandated that the board submit an audit from an outside environmental consultant to determine whether the projects the state had invested in to improve water quality were working. The audit also was meant to examine whether the state’s agriculture and natural resource agencies are doing enough to enforce water quality regulations on farms, which are the biggest source of phosphorus in Lake Champlain.

Do You Live Near Lake Champlain? Help Seven Days and ProPublica Investigate Algae Blooms.

Seven Days and ProPublica have teamed up to investigate the cleanup of Lake Champlain. Have you been affected by this issue? We’d like to hear from you.

Lake Champlain has been overloaded with phosphorus-laden runoff from farms, roads and urban sewers for decades. That pollution fuels potentially toxic blue-green algae blooms that have raised health concerns and hurt the state’s tourism industry. Under sustained pressure from citizens, environmental advocates and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Vermont’s leaders embarked on an ambitious initiative to improve the lake’s water quality, enshrined in the state’s landmark 2015 Clean Water Act.

Now, halfway through a 20-year cleanup effort mandated by the EPA, some lawmakers worry they don’t have enough information to ensure that the state is pursuing the most cost-effective cleanup strategies.

When lawmakers approved the clean water law, they took the major step of establishing a fund to pay for the cleanup and a board to administer it. Since 2016, Vermont has disbursed $928 million — $755 million in state funding and $173 million in local and federal dollars — on water quality projects and programs. That’s nearly as much as what Vermont has spent on paving and resurfacing state highways over the past decade.

As part of the law, the legislature also required the board’s leaders to provide it with a full program audit by January 2021.

But the board received no responses to an initial request for proposals in 2020. Lawmakers extended the deadline to 2023. Yet again, no outside firms bid on the audit.

Farnham said the board received informal feedback from some firms that the audit’s scope was too broad and complex. He reported back to fellow board members that he and Julie Moore, secretary of the Vermont Agency of Natural Resources, had asked legislators what to do next but didn’t receive any clear suggestions.

The board never issued a new request or revisited the matter (until Seven Days and ProPublica recently asked about it), and Vermont’s legislature never followed up to narrow the scope.

Former state Rep. David Deen, who sponsored the clean water law and retired in 2018, said he was dismayed to learn that the audit never happened.

“Personally, I find it amazing that they haven’t done that audit and that somebody in the legislature did not hold them to account to conduct that audit,” he said.

Rep. Amy Sheldon, the longtime chair of the House Committee on Environment, recalled hearing about the audit challenges but noted that it’s difficult for the legislature to follow up because Vermont’s lawmakers don’t have staff. In the other chamber, former state Sen. Chris Bray, who chaired the natural resources committee until 2025, said he did not recall hearing about the missing audit.

In an interview, Farnham acknowledged that an outside audit would be helpful. But he said the board already has robust tools for assessing progress through a yearly performance report compiled by the Vermont Department of Environmental Conservation, which coordinates and tracks most of the state’s clean water spending.

“We’ve got enough eyes coming at it from different angles that I think that mutes the need for that comprehensive audit,” he said.

The annual reporting process has improved greatly since the audit was mandated, and the DEC’s website “provides a lot of transparency,” about how the state is spending clean water money and the results, said Emily Bird, director of the department’s Water Investment Division.

But some current and former state officials say that approach isn’t a substitute for an audit to determine whether Vermont is getting adequate and cost-effective returns on its huge water quality investments.

The last independent assessment of clean water spending was a 2019 report from the state auditor. It found that a disproportionate amount of money was being spent on wastewater treatment plants, which contributed by far the smallest share of phosphorus pollution, instead of targeting bigger sources such as agriculture.

That mismatch persists seven years later. Agriculture is the largest source of phosphorus runoff, yet agricultural water quality programs receive less than a third of the total clean water funding in the current budget.

“I’d like to think they’re getting something done,” said Doug Hoffer, state auditor since 2013, referring to state agencies and legislators. “But the only way to know that is to hire someone who is independent to study that. And it’s really concerning that hasn’t been done. It really raises questions about accountability on both sides.”

An audit would do a few key things that the department’s performance reports do not, Tee Thomas, a former water finance director for the state of Vermont who now runs her own environmental consulting firm, noted via email. The reports rely on models for how effective each type of project is at reducing phosphorus. An audit would analyze water quality monitoring data from rivers and lakes to check those estimates. It would also scrutinize how well Vermont has managed projects and whether it’s gotten results, she said.

The Clean Water Fund gets, on average, $25 million to $30 million each year from the state’s rooms and meals tax, a surcharge applied to some property transfers and deposit money that consumers pay on cans and bottles. That money is paired with between $6 million and $12 million from the state’s annual capital bill, which finances infrastructure projects. The funds have gone to programs and projects to restore wetlands, expand natural buffers around fields, shore up rural roads against erosion, upgrade stormwater drains and improve manure storage on dairy farms.

The state treasurer in 2017 estimated that the cost of Vermont’s 20-year initiative would be $2.3 billion.

But finding that money could be difficult as state government spending outpaces tax revenue and cooling housing and tourism markets squeeze clean water funding sources.

Without the audit, the governor and legislators responsible for coming up with the next billion dollars’ worth of projects may not have a clear understanding of what Vermonters have gotten for the last billion, lawmakers said.

Read More

Jane Kitchel, who as longtime chair of the state Senate’s Committee on Appropriations was known for her encyclopedic knowledge of the Vermont budget, noted that a billion dollars is a significant sum for the small state. Had she not retired from the body two years ago, she said, reviving the audit “would be one of the things I’d put on my to-do list.”

The next legislative session starts in January. State Sen. Anne Watson, who chairs the Committee on Natural Resources and Energy and serves on the Committee on Appropriations, told Seven Days and ProPublica that she would likely discuss whether to revive the audit with her colleagues.

“If we value having a clean lake,” she said, “then we need to put our resources toward places that are going to make a difference, and it’s unclear to me right now that what we’re doing is effective.”

stories.title: Is the Far-Right Wave Receding?
stories.summary: But there is a deeper dissatisfaction with democracy that the far right continues to exploit. The post Is the Far-Right Wave Receding? appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Former President of Serbia Aleksandar Vucic and U.S. President Donald Trump (Anna Moneymaker-Pool/Getty Images)

Originally published in Hankyoreh .

The victory of incumbent Lula in the Brazilian presidential election was a surprise. The longtime leftist politician ran second in the first round behind far-right challenger Flavio Bolsonaro—the son of disgraced former leader Jair Bolsonaro—and no one in the history of Brazilian democracy had come from behind to win in the second round. But by mounting a huge get-out-the-vote effort, Lula defied all predictions.

Lula also defied the current trend in Latin American elections. In the last 18 months, right-wing candidates had won in seven countries, including Chile, Colombia, and Peru. The trend worldwide has been similar, with the far right winning in local elections in Germany, the extremist party of Marine Le Pen leading the polls in France, and the far right participating in governments in Italy, Finland, and the Czech Republic. Far right leaders remain in place in Russia, India, the Philippines, and, for now, Israel.

Is Lula the outlier? Or does he perhaps represent a political course correction?

For those eager to see a political wave in the making, Lula is not the only example of the electoral repudiation of the far right. On the same day as the Brazilian elections, students managed to oust the longtime autocrat Aleksandar Vucic in the equally surprising Serbian elections. Earlier this year, Viktor Orban also lost at the hands of a unified opposition. The massive “blue wave” rejection of Donald Trump in the midterm elections in the United States has continued the trend.

There is a natural feeling among voters in democratic societies to “throw the bums out.” In Latin America, a “pink” wave of progressive politicians like Ecuador’s Rafael Correa and Colombia’s Gustavo Petro has given way to a “brown” wave of ultra-conservative politicians. Voters, especially in today’s quicksilver environment of social media, respond positively to candidates who promise sweeping change. And thus, the political pendulum swings from left to right and back again.

But the far right is not just another conventional option on the political menu. It offers something radically different because it threatens to undermine the very democratic norms by which it has achieved power. In countries like Russia, Hungary, Turkey, and India, right-wing authoritarians have used democratic means—elections, constitutional changes, legal challenges—to weaken democracy. Other leaders have attempted to do away with democracy much more rapidly, as Jair Bolsonaro tried to do when he plotted to overturn the Brazilian elections that Lula won four years ago. Inspired by these rule-breakers, even traditional conservative politicians, like Yoon Suk Yeol in Korea, have attempted to suspend democracy.

And then there’s the case of Donald Trump. The U.S. president was reelected despite his efforts to overturn the 2020 elections that he lost. During his second term, he has attempted to unilaterally change the constitution. He has ignored court orders, bypassed Congress, and waged war against the mainstream media. He has repeatedly called into question the legitimacy of elections.

But Trump now has the lowest approval rating— 31 percent —of his presidency. In the midterm elections, voters rejected Trump’s party. The Democratic Party has easily retaken control of the House of Representatives, and it now has a comfortable margin of control in the Senate as well.

Unlike in Brazil, American voters are prioritizing their pocketbooks. A narrow majority of Brazilians supported Lula despite the country’s problems with debt and inflation. American voters, on the other hand, are abandoning Trump because of the economy—rising gas prices, the impact of sanctions, the consequences of the Iran War. As they demonstrated by electing Trump to a second term, many American voters don’t seem concerned about his anti-democratic rhetoric or actions.

This, more than the specific victories of the far right, is the more distressing takeaway. After all, democracy is not exactly enjoying its finest hour at the moment. Global freedom, according to the latest Freedom House report, declined for the twentieth consecutive year last year, with the United States, Bulgaria, Italy, El Salvador, and Madagascar registering significant deterioration in political and civil liberties.

Voters are turning toward anti-democratic candidates in part because they are disenchanted with democracy itself. Democratic mechanisms just don’t seem up to the task of addressing the threats currently facing the globe. Democracies have proved incapable of slowing climate change or responsibly controlling technologies like AI. Democracies have utterly failed at ensuring broad prosperity in a globalizing economy. If democrats were more successful at dealing with these problems, the far right’s promises of top-down solutions and returning to mythic pasts would not be so appealing.

This deeper problem with democracy suggests that even if the far right loses elections—in Brazil last month, the United States this week, France next year—it will not gracefully surrender the stage. Figures like Yoon Suk Yeol and Jair Bolsonaro can be jailed for their transgressions—and perhaps Trump too will follow in their footsteps. But voters will keep turning to more authoritarian alternatives if democratic institutions don’t deliver and democratic values don’t appeal.

The far right does not offer any better answers to the world’s problems. Its general response to global threats has been to turn its back. The far right supports high tariff walls, more fossil fuel extraction, and stricter controls on immigration. It repudiates all forms of globalization, lumping together neoliberal trade policies with Green energy programs and sensible approaches to immigration. The far right despises democracy not just because it puts controls on autocratic leaders but because of its association with globalization.

This, then, is the essential task of both the left and the center—to devise a new, robust internationalism that provides concrete gains to the average person while also safeguarding the planet for the next generations.

Until this happens, far-right candidates will continue to win. They might lose this or that election. But they will continue to win support with their anti-global agenda, while remaining focused on their ultimate goal of destroying democracy. They don’t want to be subject to the pendulum swings of democratic politics. They want to rip out the pendulum so that they can remain in power indefinitely.

stories.title: Brazil After the Elections
stories.summary: Is Bolsonarism over? The post Brazil After the Elections appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .

stories.body:
Flavio Bolsonaro (Shutterstock)

In Brazil, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s electoral victory over Flávio Bolsonaro on October 25 is a monumental win for the left. It could also be the start of perhaps the weakest chapter of his political career after he starts his fourth term on January 5, 2027. After all, he faces a Federal Senate (Upper House) and Chamber of Deputies (Lower House) where the Liberal Party (LP) of Bolsonaro holds the most seats.

After coming in second to Bolsonaro during the general election on October 4, Lula promised that he would get the votes from potential voters who had abstained in the first round. The interim 20 days were filled with often over-the-top appeals by both sides to their constituents.

During the televised debates, Bolsonaro used insults and baiting in his attempts to galvanize voters, appealing to their frustrations regarding corruption, crime, and Lula’s third term. In contrast and enforced by a strong social media presence, Lula used the promise of monetary payments (Pé-de-Meia Universitário) to assist college students with tuition and other expenses. He also pledged to reduce work weeks. Both of his actions might actually hurt the country economically, and they give credence to those who believe that Lula buys his votes. Lula was also bolstered by an increased street team presence (Lula’s Army), a social media footprint that was earlier hampered by Meta, and persistent anti-Trump sentiment generated by U.S. interference in South American politics.

Political scientist Gabriel Elias commented on the increase in Lula’s presence after the first-round election: “I’m feeling more optimistic today, with the massive (Worker’s Party [PT]) demonstrations we’ve seen recently. They may not have the electoral impact many are hoping for, but they leave us much better prepared to face the challenges that will come with the awful makeup of the incoming Congress.”

Reaching the People

Lula is “politically unique,” according to Daniel De Mendonça, professor of political theory at the Federal University of Pelotas. In De Mendonça’s view, Bolsonaro lost because of three main factors. The first is that the initial election focused more on Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes than on the candidates. The second is the long overdue political debates between Lula and Bolsonaro, which turned voters off because of Bolsonaro’s confrontational strategy and arrogant attitude. The third is, De Mendonça continued, Flávio ’s comments regarding the Ana Clara Soares de Oliveira case (2021) in which a military officer shot a five-year-old girl twice, killing her. Bolsonaro represented the officer in court, and this was used by Lula’s Army and spread on social media.

In the period between the two rounds, Bolsonaro had an opportunity to detail a plan for the country. Like his father, however, he offered nothing other than talk under the guise of change.

Cesar Barroso a resident of Rio de Janeiro, who voted for Bolsonaro, remarked after the election results were announced that “the lack of support from the ones [who voted] in the first round” is what lead to the upset loss. Barroso lamented that “it is very difficult to overcome a system that has been entrenched in all the country’s institutions for decades, especially in the judiciary.”

Paulo who resides in Macapá had a much more positive perspective. The election “has brought a sense of comfort to the hearts of Brazilians, who have been through so much. People from across the political spectrum—both left and right—have played a role in this journey.” He added that even members of the right support Lula in escaping from “the phenomenon of Bolsonarism.”

Steering the Ship Around?

Barring bad health, Lula will be 85 when he completes his final term. This leaves the PT with two main issues. They must find a successor and move that individual out of Lula’s shadow. Both issues may be difficult to resolve due to the corruption scandals that enveloped past candidates (e.g., Dilma Rousseff) and the sheer bombastic quality of Lula’s presence and ability to negotiate with all sides regardless of political leanings.

Political scientist Thomás Zicman de Barros described Lula as a “force of charisma,” a modern version of former President Getúlio Vargas (1930–1945, 1951–1954) who was dubbed the “Father of the Poor.” De Barros highlights that the people who truly run the country—and who refer to it as “the big center”—are all conservative local politicians and not open ideologically. This may be where Lula makes the majority of his efforts, which could lead to a lackluster fourth outing as president.

As for the Bolsonaro family, this could be the end of their political careers. The current election was always a make-or-break event for them. This latest loss might push them out of the limelight permanently.

“On Sunday night, I watched in horror as electoral fraud unfolded before my eyes,” Flávio Bolsonaro wrote after the election. “The illegitimate and illegal actions of Lula’s former lawyer allowed a mathematical impossibility to materialize, resulting in Lula gaining over 10 million votes from the first to second round.”

Instead of pushing this version of the election in the courts, Bolsonaro has fled Brazil to the relative safety of his brother Eduardo in South Florida—despite Justice Alexandre de Moraes request for his passport prior to his exodus. Bolsonaro complained that this action was part of making him “a hostage” and an “object of blackmail to protect the corrupt Supreme Court justices from impeachment.” Whether this will lead to a campaign to contest the election is currently unclear. There has been a large drop-off in content on Bolsonaro-related media.

One prominent Bolsonaro remains in the country. Michelle de Paula Bolsonaro, wife of Jair Bolsonaro, won her first Senate seat in Brasilia D.F. during the first round. She may be the one to watch out for, especially if she starts eyeing the presidential position.

Brazilians still deeply distrust the government. That and the greater precarity of the workforce are the two biggest challenges facing Brazil. As De Barros points out, the normal political climate is not just “about politicians getting rich. It’s also economic elites working with the state and with politicians to get rich.” An authoritarian leader could appeal to future voters on an anti-corruption platform.

The Future of Brazil

Shortly after the election results were released, Trump both stated that he “did not want to take sides” but felt that it looked like a “rigged” election. Bolsonaro thanked him and the American people, stating that “President Trump is a great defender of freedom and expression.”

Beyond insults, jabs regarding organized crime, and tariffs, Trump will largely back off. With most of South America already under his influence and no other opportunities being available during the remainder of his term, Brazil is relatively safe from foreign interference.

Brazilians are generally hostile to Trump’s efforts to intervene in Brazilian politics. But they also recognize the advantages of a good relationship with Washington. “We are living through a different kind of war—a war of agreements,” a person from Sáo Pablo told me. “Brazil is expanding through bilateral deals; we have agreements with a large part of the world. We’re the friend to everyone.”

Could he could see Brazil working with the United States under Lula? “Access to American infrastructure would certainly help with capital, but what about the social aspect?” he responded.

stories.title: In Praise Of Japan’s Failure To Keep Up
stories.summary: The post In Praise Of Japan’s Failure To Keep Up appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The country was told it needed to be more like Silicon Valley to compete, but its refusal may have left it better placed to decide what technology is actually for.

Journalist and broadcaster Michael Fitzpatrick has run with all the big game of journalism while inhabiting more countries than is absolutely necessary.

TOKYO — Nothing triggers the bog-walloping Fenian in me quite like a visit to the British Embassy. This one, with its fine Georgian-revival facade, looked on my last visit a decade ago like a lost Cotswold manor-house brought to life in Tokyo.

But what was it that I found so unsettling? Perhaps the stately setting? Or its gilt-framed displays of a preternaturally regal, late queen? Her gaze following me about the room as I moved among the fine art and mahogany, like those creepy Sacred Heart of Jesus portraits I grew up with. Me, a lad reared in an Irish republican home where the Queen’s annual Christmas messages were as welcome as a poltergeist.

To the more clubbable, the embassy’s English country house manner would have seemed merely civilized; a demonstration that Merrie England had acquired over generations the ability to arrange the upholstery without the aid of an AI shepherd.

The decor was a projection of centuries of British self-assuredness and ease, distilling, as adroitly as the form allows, the essence of (an ebbing) sovereign power. The fine art, damask and agreeable lighting gave no hint that Britain’s technological might has long migrated elsewhere. That such hegemony now lies with American platforms and Asian supply chains. But the genius of spaces like these is that you can start to believe in a type of fanciful continuity of the imperishable.

It inveigles you into sharing a fantasy. This one being that if these old arrangements had survived war, decolonization, Tamagotchis and the mobile phone, perhaps it might survive the latest digital convulsions, too. Here was a refuge, some autonomy even, from the technological superpowers that increasingly own us. Proof that small jurisdictions of taste, privacy and human-scale abound.

Of course, like any contemporary state, the British must put on a show of modernity. Outside the embassy hung long banners declaring that England was now a “Unicorn Kingdom.” But from where I was standing, the oak heart of this very British establishment demurred. They had seen it all before. But it was co-opting some of Silicon Valley’s grandiose illusions just to be safe. Inside the older, more powerful unicorns of mythology resided sinewy on the royal coat of arms. Not just representing rarity, but purity and extreme ferocity, reminding me of some English public-schoolboys I knew.

But this is the great charm of the embassy interior — its refusal to update. Even in the face of economic realities and the dark, immutable forces that forge them. Here was a stand for the moral and institutional habits of our ancestors.

A Sinking Feeling

Big Tech oligarchs can threaten to transform all that is before them, but the timeless endurance of this lived-in aristocratic grandeur will survive, I was starting to feel. Now I — sinking in someone else’s club chair — was beginning to get it.

Assailed by crypto pirates, the succubi of VC-led extractor corporatism and the crumbling of knowledge work , we feel profoundly the foundations of power shifting ominously beneath us. Countering that are the Embassy’s older, time-tested values and their comforting familiarity. People like the faddish Steve Jobs would probably have hated it. Like death for Californians, he thought furniture was optional.

Beyond the embassy precincts, Japan too was stealing itself from Darwinian upheaval, slouching toward it from across the Pacific. That was 10 years ago. Now the evolution has landed, proposing a shotgun wedding with a prenuptial dubbed Pax Silica.

The vow is simple: Join our techno view of the world or be made irrelevant by it.

Or you can do what the embassy valiantly attempts: indulge in wishful thinking that we are beholden to no one; sovereign power is unassailable and will prevail over any forces that seek to unseat it. Look! We have brass sconces! Damask pelmets!

Eventually, I allowed myself to be consoled, finding one of the ambassador’s snugglers, an oversized armchair, to sink into and reflect. Besides, despite residues of unease, it was too late to bolt. The mayor of London, Boris Johnson at the time, had been promised forth — attended by the nation’s press and its tech somebodies — to expand on a subject without any obvious tripwire: London’s thrusting home-grown cashless tech.

I had a fancy I might know better. As a former hack himself, Johnson knew how to give good copy, and I had an uncharitable thought he would not disappoint.

After all, Johnson had already just snot-o-grammed a schoolboy in a game of mock rugby the day before. Metaphors for the bumbling, bruiser foreigner riding roughshod over finer Japanese sensibilities came tumbling off the press. And why not? We in the geographical West have plenty of form here.

“Japan too was stealing itself from Darwinian upheaval, slouching toward it from across the Pacific. That was 10 years ago.”

Polite rebuffs, coded rebukes, and death threats from Japan aimed at preventing Johnny Foreigner from putting his size-12 welly through the shoji doors have often proved futile over the centuries. We were never much good at taking the hint.

It fell to U.S. Navy Commodore Matthew C. Perry in 1853 to finally dash aside Japan’s isolationist polite “Please Do Not Disturb” sign to demand, with menaces, access rights. Included in the list of “diplomatic” offerings was a white flag, should the Japanese ever feel the need to employ it.

Almost touchingly British, this American politely tapping on the door while carrying a battering ram. And echoing today’s political realities, when faced with “having no cards,” capitulation must follow as night follows day.

Can’t Put A Good Man Down

Now we had a capering politician on a trade mission to Japan for whom such blundering was just a warm-up act. Japan’s wall of unassailable, face-saving etiquette would ensure his next gaffe.

Johnson was on his pins, grandly pitching the City Boys’ latest Fintech triumph — its “light-years ahead” magical, cashless payments tech. The marvelous BRITISH tech in question was contactless IC (integrated circuit) cards, which made paying for travel on the tube absolute duck soup.

Pausing to ask rhetorically, “Who else can boast that?” he practically invited an intervention. And so … apostle of truth that I am, I did not hold back. From the press seats, I pointed out that Japanese travelers were largely already there should they wish it. Japan had had the cashless tech for years, and practically single-handedly conjured up the tech in question while others fumbled for dimes. A couple of years back, I had even completed a journey — with mixed results, I have to say — around Japan to try out humanity’s first tentative steps toward going cashless.

Obviously, no news of this had reached the British capital, or the ears of the mayor’s flunkies, because suddenly Johnson looked all in, spluttering into his cuffs: “Really, is this true!?” A sea of dark heads bobbed in assent.

“Have I just undermined the whole raison d’être of this event? So, what is my raison d’être for being here?” he queried, eyeing his aides. “Why was I not told this?”

Summing up the possibilities, I arrived at a few rapid deductions. Firstly, his immediate staff and the embassy had signally failed to do their homework. Secondly, too many of his hosts were equally bereft of the facts concerning their own country’s digital prowess in this matter.

Third, and most crucially, a naked emperor, no matter how richly deserving of exposure, is still an Emperor in Japan; only on pain of social death should he be confronted with the humiliating truth.

It was an object lesson in the terrifying extremes to which Japan is willing to take its impeccable manners. Selling coals to Newcastle may be ill-advised, but apparently in Japan the correct form is for Newcastle to politely deny the existence of its coal pits in the face of such magnificent British magnanimity.

Yet this gaffe can be forgiven, if only because the Japanese themselves were largely in the dark about their own tech — having long refused to trust anything but hard cash. Because of this typical national recalcitrance, the contactless technology perfected in Japan decades ago initially went nowhere , no matter how hard any Japanese Boris Johnsons tried to push it. It was only after the tech took off in Europe and elsewhere in the 2000s that it gained a widespread local following.

The Root Of All Evil Is Progress

For me, this became a quiet symbol of the failure of progress and of our rightful reluctance to submit unconditionally to its tyranny. A new tyranny that demands societies adapt to every new technology. But as Japan proved, we do not have to. The fact that Japanese innovation remained so entirely invisible, even to the fintech envoys themselves, is also symptomatic of how Japan’s tech research routinely fails to achieve a global impact commensurate with its genius.

What is missing, as is so often the case in Japan, is the aggressive cultural machinery required to turn raw research into a bankable international asset.

The country lacks, above all, the cultural instinct to shout its name from the rooftops. When advised to do so, heads are patiently shaken in agreement, and eventually, it’s determined that no shoestring is too threadbare for the task. Even the most prestigious startup factory at Tokyo University has only one part-time PR rep. She does not speak English.

“What is missing, as is so often the case in Japan, is the aggressive cultural machinery required to turn raw research into a bankable international asset.”

Consequently, there is very little understanding of how global visibility is created.

Treating communications, international business development and storytelling as peripheral administrative functions suggests a genuine contradiction here. Universities are being ordered to create globally competitive companies but seem blind to the fact that they are institutionally unsuited for the task. After observing such behavior time and time again in Japan, the communications gap is glaringly real.

Could such attitudes be an atavistic return to the days when storytellers, entertainers and the like were classified under Japan’s feudal caste system as literally “ hinin ” non-humans?

A suspicion, not unwarranted, that marketing and PR, like all stories, are a kind of … lies. Manipulative ones at that. When I asked about the story from these cloistered university startup hubs, the basic reply was, “Anyway, what use is a mere ‘story’ when you have specs!?”

Was this where Japan was failing startup-wise? I wondered.

Never Losing The Plod

A few years later, I think I heard my answer: “It’s not about the tech, it’s about the execution,” explained one Tokyo tech insider at a startup meeting.

Where Japan often fails, he continued, was the slow pace of business. He was right. Japanese commerce likes to plod, and the Japanese are inveterate plodders. Decisions take months, even years, to kick things around, assess, assess, assess, then slowly “build trust” for the sake of “nemawashi” (preparations).

Japan’s sluggish adoption of cashless payments perfectly illustrated this trend. What was lost on its hapless Japanese inventors and investors was that they alone held the keys and were the legislators and instigators of a powerful new digital tool that the Tech Tyrants across the ocean had failed to monopolize.

Londoners, forever with an eye out for every angle, understood better. Fintech of this ilk being perhaps its only success yet at stemming a tide of American tech dominance, there was much to harumph about. While not a wholly British success story, it was about the only Big Tech triumph the UK could cling to before burlier Fin-Tech Bros sharp-elbowed them back to their country estates.

In the face of it, Japan and the UK seem powerless to stop this leaking away of sovereignty. Japan’s puzzling foot-dragging on the tech illustrates an overlooked aspect of its innovation drive — its long history of brilliant innovations that were, for various reasons, overlooked and sidetracked. It also illustrates very well Japan’s institutional-character problem and its uncanny ability to turn wine into water.

Opportunity Knocks

It was Toyota that ushered me into one of its first commercial electric cars 30 years ago. Ditto, a self-driving vehicle that same year. Thanks to a “mad-scientist dream” for humanoid robots, a Japanese computer scientist told me 15 years ago that her country led the world in AI machine learning. Now, like Japan’s version of the Rip Van Winkle tale, Taro Urashima, the nation is waking up to find it overslept in all these fields.

Its less cautious neighbors, famously, ran with the tech Japan had been quietly pioneering, leaving the country on the wrong side of a technological divide entirely of its own making. The American giants, meanwhile, rose rapidly, ate everyone else’s lunch, pocketed their dinner money and now appear to be talking options on any future breathing plans others may be foolishly having.

That’s why we rant about Amazon, Apple, Meta, and the like as tech’s “Magnificent Seven,” and not the Seven Samurai. Contemporary Japan simply often fails to capitalize on, or communicate, its genius.

China, too, is leaving Japan and the rest of us at the bedroom door. It may have gotten its lead by “distilling” all the best ideas from Japan and elsewhere, but China is now outpacing us with the speed it has put these applications to use.

Ask any savvy Japanese, “How so?” and they’ll evoke the “Galápagos” theory. Like the plants and creatures on those famous islands, Japan’s tech standards and business practices have developed a unique character incompatible with overseas wants and desires.

Even the country’s myriad startups throw up lots of weird and wonderful concepts only seen in Japan, earning them domestic fans but a condemned death march if tempted to ship abroad due to their lack of marketing savvy and other entrepreneurial qualities. Because to grow globally, Japan lacks the linguistic skills, overengineers its products and fails to understand what might play well abroad. Nor is it an accident that Japanese researchers boast the most recipients of the Ig Nobel prizes, an annual satirical award presented by the “Annals of Improbable Research” science humor magazine.

“Japan’s puzzling foot-dragging on the tech illustrates an overlooked aspect of its innovation drive — its long history of brilliant innovations that were, for various reasons, overlooked and sidetracked.”

A New Kind Of Innovation

There was even a craze called Chindōgu for what became known as useless “curious or strange tools,” in the ‘80s and ‘90s when Japan actually made stuff the world wanted.

This Galápagosian inward focus, while fostering some unique innovations, has also left Japan isolated in the global tech landscape, or so the thinking goes. This created a superficially hi-tech Japan, Hideki Onda, a former Apple director, once told me.

Onda believed Japan’s deeply cautious and conservative business and political classes were the root cause. This allowed Japan to evolve along Galápagos lines because the ruthless nature of startup capitalism and radical technocratic disruption was such a poor fit for Japan’s slower, more considered way of doing things.

When economists were chivying for the re-ignition of Japan’s competitive “animal spirits,” the country responded with its trademark animal caution.

To best illustrate this, Onda recalled a time in 1996 when Apple was pushing Japan to introduce its teaching tech to schools. The education minister’s answer was a polite “Kekko desu,” or no.

Apple’s then-CEO Michael Spindler asked Onda when they might return to try again. “When the ‘60s-era floor indicator above the ministry’s elevator door goes digital,” Onda told him.

A decisively Luddite response, many thought at the time. But fast-forward through 30 years of digitization, and we are seeing method in the minister’s madness. The rush to digitization and the digital economy, we found belatedly, has resulted in its own casualties .

The American models of capital efficiency and market disruption we so admired are now being seen as possibly ruinous. We are learning, for one, that networked screen-based learning is no silver bullet. Nor do all cultures suit the startup models; just ask the equal-with-Japan on social-cohesion-first Swedes. Read Noema in print.

The Medium Is The Message

After noting a drop in student literacy, Sweden has now reversed its push toward digital learning. Cellphones have been banned in schools, and the textbook industry rejoices at schools’ return to paper.

And yet the assault from a proselytizing Big Tech on Japan, where digitization has been slow and AI remains largely a curiosity in the workplace, is intensifying.

There is still an unfulfilled desire to digitize; that is true. Broadcast mainly from some business quarters and certain politicos. Japan’s AI regulations, for instance, have been made as loose as those in the U.S., and many see them as an incentive for American corporations to move in.

I asked a Japanese friend and tech journalist what he thought about this new “Black Ships” moment, and he told me he expects an awkward culture clash of Titanic proportions. “Because American technology companies are often extraordinarily irresponsible about the social consequences of what they build.”

He had another keen observation for me: “Ultimately, Silicon Valley is not primarily optimized to maximize human wellbeing. It is optimized to maximize returns.”

Japan. Ostensibly capitalistic, has a rather different take. The emphasis is on social cohesion, not profits. This contrast is not simply cultural. In a 2006 Japanese government survey, nearly 70% of responding Japanese companies said employees were important stakeholders, and 90% planned to maintain long-term employment.

He now suspects that when we look back several decades, or perhaps several centuries, from now, we may conclude that our current tech revolution produces too much “technological pollution” — innovations that ultimately caused considerable suffering to large numbers of people despite Silicon Valley’s innovative bent. This is particularly daunting in light of well-informed concerns that AI development will lead to our extinction.

His conclusion echoes Japan’s nascent clarion call for “technological sovereignty.” It is now the responsibility, not of America, but of countries with long histories and deep cultural traditions such as in Europe, Japan and elsewhere, to propose ways of using technology that engage much more seriously with social responsibility, he argues.

And it is true that some Europeans and Japanese are now working to reduce their dependency on U.S. tech. But when you don’t have the cards, a certain raspy voice likes to remind us, the white flag your pushy competitors hand you can seem like a lifesaver after all.

Techno Darwinism Dawns

Until the triumph of such heretics, the inescapable dark logic of techno Darwinism gets to cast its shade far into Japan’s corridors of power for now. Supping with the Devil as a hedge against total irrelevance, you might want to call it. Just bring long chopsticks and hope you are not on the menu.

“The rush to digitization and the digital economy, we found belatedly, has resulted in its own casualties.”

Presiding over national decline and a plummeting yen, Peter Thiel’s recent appearance in Tokyo must have seemed an omen of sorts to the government — perhaps even an opportunity. Certainly, Japan’s premier Sanae Takaichi received Thiel and his trade mission cheerfully enough, despite any whiff of sulfur. Besides being something of a missionary from the darker side of the Singularity faithful, his visit was the latest in a long list of tech emissaries from across the water. U.S. venture capital, too, is arriving fast. Marc Andreessen , boss of one of the heftiest firms, opened his first overseas office in Japan this summer. It is no secret that Japan now sees the Silicon Valley model as the one that might get it out of its considerable hole.

Brandon Hill, founder of an outfit that helps startups on both sides of the Pacific, told me Tokyo is desperate for more startups and more “successful exits.” The hope is that those eager entrepreneurs will spark another period of rapid reinvention like the 19th-century’s Meiji-era modernization, or Japan’s dramatic re-industrialization after World War II. This one, we imagine, will be driven by homegrown Silicon-Valley wannabes with less perishable wings of wax.

But Japan should be thinking beyond simply creating more startups, Hill insists, keen to impart to an attentive Japan the magic formula: “It should be creating more globally competitive companies.”

Death March, What Death March?

But these are death march orders again. Because given Japan’s current climate of anxiety and its lack of survival skills, English and narrative nous, the global market will exact its toll. Once a nation of outward-looking, inveterate tinkerers willing to make technology central to national survival, the collapse of the ‘80s economic boom in 1991 led to lost decades and economic stagnation. The bust also created a fear of risk-taking and a retreat into safe jobs, safe investments and safe conservative governments.

Thanks to that trauma, contemporary Japan is a much more inward-looking and risk-averse place now. The bubble’s collapse and the financial crisis that followed gave way to a long corporate decline. In a 2024 survey , the Bank of Japan found that many firms had curbed investment and built cash reserves after the crisis and later shocks. That history helps explain business caution, though it cannot by itself explain Japan’s wider inward turn.

The moral and institutional habits formed by Japan’s lost decades are unlikely to evaporate at the urging of a few Tech Valley gurus. Many here, perhaps rightly, take pride that the Libertarian, go-getting style of the buccaneering new world capitalists remains as rare as buttered sushi.

Despite this, some sections of central government, such as the bullish Ministry of Economy, are insisting the nation pledges its shirt to such a miraculous resurrection of entrepreneurial spirits. Even if it means the much-dreaded importing — however imperfectly — of alien business practices, plus accommodating the Devil of foreign investment and all its stratagems.

The current thinking is, if Japan’s satraps are to become Satan’s latest freshly minted imps so that the country can flourish, so be it. Accordingly, Japan’s ministries must undergo a Damascene conversion, buckle under for universal digitization, get with the program and ditch the fax for the splendid shining lie of the startup. Strong medicine for a nation that swears by “not waking the baby.”

The Revolution Will Not Be Commodified

As already mentioned, the revolution will not be restricted to business. Shanghaied into the program are its universities, too, to be raided for startup recruits. They now giddily employ the magic word salads of “incubators,” “ecosystems” and “unicorns” — incantations in the newly imported, and hopefully profitable, cargo cult.

In service to the “Stack” — the secret sauce of the vaunted digital product — they must dump the Old-Fogey seats of learning/babysitting roles and learn to “hyper-scale.” And in doing so, become the engines of a “new technology-driven nation” where science and technology provide economic growth and national security. The model is California’s lucrative fusion of pioneering lab work and entrepreneurship stripped for export.

This is a big ask for an institution whose principal role, until now, was an untaxing refuge for students lately overtaxed by Japan’s notorious entrance exams.

But the heart wants what the heart wants. So out must go the playground-cum-finishing school model applied to the young before they join the workforce. It is a system that makes them easy targets for job automation anyway.

“The moral and institutional habits formed by Japan’s lost decades are unlikely to evaporate at the urging of a few Tech Valley gurus.”

Research at the top universities is another matter entirely. World-class and innovative but sheltered from the worldly West Coast-style monetizing of know-how, they are an unlikely vehicle for commerce. But to the trendier, more tech-savvy of Tokyo’s mandarins, gifting academic researchers with money and startup blueprints must seem like a foolproof remedy for Japan’s economic woes.

The country’s economic emergency is real enough. Japan’s nominal GDP, which once ranked second in the world, fell to third place in 2010 and then to fourth place in 2023. The country’s share of global nominal GDP has fallen sharply, from approximately 18% in 1995 to approximately 3.8% in 2025. More worryingly, its nominal GDP per capita has also fallen from second in the world to 38th today.

Real wages have stagnated for 30 years; the yen has fallen to a low not seen for nearly 40 years.

Ingredients But No Recipe

But there are reasons for hope. After all, the country has all the ingredients to make it a supreme techno-state. Elite scientists, a magic-money spigot (take a bow, quantitative easing and near-zero interest rates) and world-class manufacturing chops.

But instead of impacting our world with its surprisingly useful research applications, the policies, as my tech writer friend pointed out, are only exposing an almighty clash of civilizations. It’s another institutional mismatch where Japanese universities, slow and hierarchical to their bones, repurpose poorly as startup factory incubators (which must be fast and unstable). The friction is almost palpable.

After decades of being left to their own insular devices — including, bizarrely, a reluctance to publish abroad — university-linked founders are now lining up to take grants for “global startups” while conveniently skipping the global part. No slogan has ever been emptier than “be global from the start,” as most of these founders don’t speak English .

But without the “ go global !” declaration, they would be unlikely to qualify for funding. This makes Japan’s latest bid to race across borders, like all its other vaunted internationalization schemes, a sham.

Because Japan lingers in the bottom ranks of English proficiency tests and belatedly adopts international marketing practices, like pitching or self-promotion, its innovation remains mostly invisible to a broader public.

Without a sudden sea-change, conjuring national self-reliance, economic security and cutting-edge innovation out of Japan’s unbelievably stuffy, risk-averse and archaic institutions will be a miracle. Already, in critical fields like AI, semiconductors and defense tech, the chance to lead sailed away with the last of the country’s frustrated emigre innovators.

Enter The Zombies

But appealing fictions have a habit of overriding the stark facts. So universities take a substantial amount of government money to pump out startups despite being poorly equipped to produce global-ready startups as the state is requesting. Most of these universities focus on Japan’s stockpile of zombie enterprises — the kinds that have stayed alive thanks to cheap credit and government handouts rather than healthy, global market performance.

Japanese startups outside the blessed and coddled circle of academia fare no better. Lacking the swagger of Silicon Valley, Japan’s corporate culture is the antithesis of America’s individualistic, T-shirted tycoons. Japan’s corporate culture prioritizes conformist don’t-rock-the-boat mediocrity, uses generalists rather than specialists, and favors risk-aversion over disruptive ideas; monetizing innovation will remain a struggle. The Economist suggests Tokyo’s “startups first” growth plan looks woefully misguided.

Not that the country lacks the kind of Promethean chutzpah that could bring new light, energy and progress. But Japan has a habit of taking the role of an angry Zeus — chaining any unruly innovators to the nearest rock. Japan has a long list of disgruntled innovators who feel hard done by its corporate system. Even the chap who invented the white LED, Shuji Nakamura , was originally rewarded with a corporate bonus of just 20,000 yen (roughly $200 at the time).

Scapegoat

If there is one man famous for bringing raw, individualistic U.S.-style techno-capitalism to these shores and failing spectacularly, it is Takefumi Horie — AKA “Horiemon.” No fire-bearing Titan to mankind is he — more an ambitious internet provider — but instructive all the same was the treatment of this tech startup founder imprisoned for 21 months for his disruptive antics a couple of decades ago.

Horie’s style put him at the center of a culture clash between U.S. and Japanese business. He became the scourge of Japanese companies when his internet firm Livedoor launched a hostile bid for Nippon Broadcasting in 2005. Using a legal loophole in off-hours trading, it bought 29.6% of the radio broadcaster in one go, bringing its holding to around a third. It was an attempt to take control of the powerful Fuji TV. The move led the government to change the Securities and Exchange law to extend takeover rules to off-hours trading. The bid failed.

“Japan’s corporate culture prioritizes conformist don’t-rock-the-boat mediocrity, uses generalists rather than specialists, and favors risk-aversion over disruptive ideas; monetizing innovation will remain a struggle.”

Authorities arrested Horie a year later on a separate issue. He faced charges that his company Livedoor falsified financial results to mislead investors. The company reported a pretax profit of about 5 billion yen, but prosecutors said it had actually made a loss of about 300 million yen. Horie was convicted of securities-law violations and sentenced to 2 ½ years in prison, serving about 21 months.

Such treatment shocked Japan’s startup community and signaled that non-consensus-driven, Anglo-Saxon, morally ambiguous capitalism bent on erasing cultural norms might be tolerated in the U.S. but punished in Japan. Japanese tech startups aiming to be the tallest poppy at the time quickly pulled up their roots. The startup revolution and rush to digitization were canceled.

In the face of Japan’s bureaucratic top-down planning, Japan’s elite universities, patient capital and strong manufacturing record count for little. Fast-moving, software-driven global tech trends simply move on — too quickly for a Japanese catch-up.

This, despite Japan actually sharing the passion for tech America does. In the field of AI in particular, Japan’s affair with machine intelligence is relatively long and productive. Computer scientist Noriko Arai sat me down in her office 15 years ago and explained how a “mad scientist” dream of humanoid robots placed Japan ahead in the AI race decades ago.

In the 1980s, while Western researchers were still skeptical of neural networks, Japanese scientists were diving deep into artificial neurons and machine learning. “We say Japan was ahead at the time,” AI researcher Yutaka Matsuo told me. “But perhaps that doesn’t mean a lot now.”

Japan fell behind, failing to catch the St. Vitus’s dance deemed necessary to animate a Silicon Valley-style digital resurrection. But perhaps we have been measuring the wrong thing. Yes, its institutions are often too conservative to change, but as we survey the damage that technology has inflicted upon us, were the plodders right to plod?

Fearlessness in the face of failure, rapid iteration, global self-confidence, impatience with hierarchy — are definitively not the country’s house style. But because of this, did Japan eventually dodge a bullet? My tech journalist friend and others like him increasingly feel so.

There are fears of a too-rapidly deployed foreign AI risk, fears over the erosion of social cohesion, fears that a gig economy will replace Japan’s cherished full employment. The call is also for more strategic autonomy from tech corporations who are outmaneuvering the locals.

Black Ships Redux

But the chatter is not just of another Black Ships “coup” or “digital colonialism” if Japan adopts the American model of rapid disruption. There’s a growing realization that the friction of the culture clash is perhaps a benefit. Japan’s plodding ways and institutions incompatible with hyper-capitalism offer a chance to install some kind of rugged technological sovereignty. They allow Japan to escape the technological determinism now infecting the West.

The appearance of a technology doesn’t mean that societies are suddenly forced to adapt to it. Societies should decide which technologies to adopt, how quickly, under what rules and for whose benefit. In 2021, UNESCO called for human oversight and demanded that we give societies a basis to accept or reject AI systems. A call now responded to belatedly by institutions and governments worldwide, mirroring people’s concerns over AI developments.

Coincidentally, Johnson’s ill-timed Fintech speech I attended at the embassy shines a light on the assumption that every problem has a technological solution, and that more technology necessarily means progress. A technological determinism and the myth of technological progressiveness Japan should be keen to avoid.

“We have to recognize that disruptive technology is simply inevitable and we cannot put the technological genie back in the bottle,” Johnson added to his contactless payments pitch. “Once the toothpaste is out of the tube, folks, that’s it.”

Inertia Is Not All Bad News

Do the Japanese need to become more Californian to be more capable, or should these old institutions and Japan’s inertia be left alone to create some breathing space? Bill Gates said recently there is “no plan to ease the entry into the AI era.” Perhaps Japan’s experience of friction at that very entry is telling us something. Despite its half-hearted attempts to mimic Silicon Valley values, the country’s deep inertia seems to be buffeting it from some of the ill effects of globalization and technological disruption.

For decades, Japanese companies have attempted to shield their workers from the insatiable demands of stockholders and capital as part of a “social responsibility” mindset to help create jobs and safeguard companies.

“As outdated and sluggish as the nation’s institutions might be, their limbic caution has preserved livelihoods.”

As outdated and sluggish as the nation’s institutions might be, their limbic caution has preserved livelihoods. Because, as it has often been said, Japan is a massive job creation scheme. Any introduction of American-style lean capitalism would threaten the labor policies aimed at creating overemployment, and the men I see guiding traffic around roadworks outside my house where a traffic light would do would all be out of a job. Making Japan a possible, and unlikely, last stand to our current reckoning with technological determinism.

Everywhere else the old rules are breaking, and some are heading for the exit laden with unicorn silver. West Coast billionaires are even reportedly seeking escape hatches or bunkers. Could tardy Japan be on their list of hideaways?

Exchange Tokyo for Vienna in this old joke and you’ll see what I mean. “If the world should ever come to an end — move to Vienna, because everything there happens 20 years later,” goes the quip used even today about the celestial city.

Japan is not unlike Vienna in this respect in its refusal to update. And its failure to do so, like the unabashed, unreconstructed British Embassy in Tokyo, may not be a disadvantage at all. On the contrary, it can remind us of what we value, and why.
